subtopic: Electric Charges and Their Basic Properties
stem: How much positive and negative charge is present in 1gm of water? How many electrons are present in it? Given, molecular mass of water is 18.0 g.
solution:
Molecular mass of water is 18.0 gm, that means the number of molecules in 18.0 gm of water is \(6.02 \times 10^{23}\).
\(\therefore\) Number of molecules in 1gm of water \(= 6.02 \times 10^{23}/18\). One molecule of water (H\(_{2}\)O) contains two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom. Thus the number of electrons in H\(_{2}\)O is sum of the number of electrons in H\(_{2}\) and oxygen. There are 2 electrons in H\(_{2}\) and 8 electrons oxygen.
\(\therefore\) Number of electrons in H\(_{2}\)O \(= 2+8 = 10\).
Total number of protons / electrons in 1.0 gm of water \(= \dfrac{6.02 \times 10^{23}}{18} \times 10 = 3.34 \times 10^{23}\)
Total positive charge \(= 3.34 \times 10^{23} \times\) charge on a proton
\(= 3.34 \times 10^{23} \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\) C \(= 5.35 \times 10^{4}\) C
This positive charge is balanced by equal amount of negative charge so that the water molecule is electrically neutral.

subtopic: Electric Charges and Their Basic Properties
stem: Charge on an electron is \(1.6 \times 10^{-19}\) C. How many electrons are required to accumulate a charge of one coulomb?
solution:
\(1.6 \times 10^{-19}\) C \(= 1\) electron
\(\therefore 1C = \dfrac{1}{1.6 \times 10^{-19}}\) electrons
\(= 0.625 \times 10^{19} = 6.25 \times 10^{18}\) electrons
\(6.25 \times 10^{18}\) electrons are required to accumulate a charge of one coulomb.

stem: Calculate and compare the electrostatic and gravitational forces between two protons which are \(10^{-15}\) m apart. Value of \(G = 6.674 \times 10^{-11}\) m\(^{3}\) kg\(^{-1}\) s\(^{-2}\) and mass of the proton is \(1.67 \times 10^{-27}\) kg
solution:
The electrostatic force between the protons is given by \(F_{e} = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}}\dfrac{q_{1}q_{2}}{r^{2}}\)
Here, \(q_{1} = q_{2} = +1.6 \times 10^{-19}\) C, \(r = 10^{-15}\) m
\(\therefore F_{e} = 9 \times 10^{9}\dfrac{(1.6 \times 10^{-19})(1.6 \times 10^{-19})}{(10^{-15})^{2}}\)
\(= 9 \times 1.6 \times 1.6 \times 10^{1}\) N
\(F_{e} = 2.3 \times 10^{2}\) N  --- (10.8.a)
The gravitational force between the protons is given by
\(F_{g} = G\dfrac{m_{1}m_{2}}{r^{2}}\)
\(= \dfrac{6.674 \times 10^{-11} \times 1.67 \times 10^{-27} \times 1.67 \times 10^{-27}}{(10^{-15})^{2}}\)
\(F_{g} = 1.86 \times 10^{-34}\) N  --- (10.8.b)
Comparing 10.8. (a) and 10.8.(b)
\(\dfrac{F_{e}}{F_{g}} = \dfrac{2.30 \times 10^{-2}\ \text{N}}{1.86 \times 10^{-34}\ \text{N}} = 1.23 \times 10^{36}\)
Thus, the electrostatic force is about 36 orders of magnitude stronger than the gravitational force.

stem: Three charges of 2\(\mu\)C, 3\(\mu\)C and 4\(\mu\)C are placed at points A, B and C respectively, as shown in Fig. a. Determine the force on A due to other charges.
solution:
Given,
AB \(= 4.0\) cm, BC \(= 3.0\) cm
\(\therefore\) AC \(= \sqrt{4^{2}+3^{2}} = 5.0\) cm
Magnitude of force \(\vec{F}_{AB}\) on A due to B is,
\(\vec{F}_{AB} = \left(\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}}\right)\dfrac{2 \times 10^{-6} \times 3 \times 10^{-6}}{(4 \times 10^{-2})^{2}}\)
\(= \dfrac{9 \times 10^{9} \times 6}{16 \times 10^{-4}} \times 10^{-12}\)
\(= 3.37 \times 10\)
\(= 33.7\) N
This force acts at point A and is directed along \(\overrightarrow{BA}\) (Fig. (b)).
Magnitude of force \(\vec{F}_{AC}\) on A due to C is,
\(\vec{F}_{AC} = \left(\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}}\right)\dfrac{2 \times 10^{-6} \times 4 \times 10^{-6}}{(5 \times 10^{-2})^{2}}\)
\(= \dfrac{9 \times 10^{9} \times 8.0 \times 10^{-12}}{25 \times 10^{-4}}\)
\(= \dfrac{72}{25} \times 10 = 28.8\) N
This force acts at point A and is directed along \(\overrightarrow{CA}\). (Fig. 10.6.(b))
\(\vec{F} = \vec{F}_{AB} + \vec{F}_{AC}\)
Magnitude of resultant force is,
\(F = \left[F_{AC}^{2} + F_{AB}^{2} + 2F_{AC} \cdot F_{AB} \cdot \cos\theta\right]^{1/2}\)
\(= 59.3\) N
Using Eq. (2.10) calculating \(\tan\alpha\), \(\alpha = 16.93^{0}\)
Direction of the resultant force is \(16.9^{\circ}\) north of west. (Fig. c)

subtopic: Electric Field and Lines of Force
stem: Gap between two electrodes of the spark-plug used in an automobile engine is 1.25 mm. If the potential of 20 V is applied across the gap, what will be the magnitude of electric field between the electrodes?
solution:
\(E = \dfrac{V}{d}\)
\(E = \dfrac{20V}{1.25 \times 10^{-3}m} = 16 \times 10^{-3} = 1.6 \times 10^{4}\dfrac{V}{m}\)
This electric field is sufficient to ionize the gaseous mixture of fuel compressed in the cylinder and ignite it.

subtopic: Electric Field and Lines of Force
stem: Three point charges are placed at the vertices of a right isosceles triangle as shown in the Fig. a. What is the magnitude and direction of the resultant electric field at point P which is the mid point of its hypotenuse?
solution:
Electric field is the force an a unit positive charge, the fields at P due to the charges at A, B and C are shown in the Fig. b. \(\vec{E}_{A}\) is the field at P due to charge at A and \(\vec{E}_{C}\) is the field at P due to charge at C. Since P is the midpoint of AC and the fields at A and C are equal in magnitudes and are opposite in direction, \(\vec{E}_{A} = -\vec{E}_{C}\). \(\vec{E}_{A} + \vec{E}_{C} = 0\). Thus, the field at P is only to the charge at B and can be written as
\(\vec{E}_{p} = \vec{E}_{B} = \dfrac{2 \times 10^{-6}}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}(BP)^{2}}\)
\(\vec{E}_{p} = \dfrac{2 \times 10^{-6} \times 9 \times 10^{9}}{(5/\sqrt{2})^{2}}\)
\(= \dfrac{2 \times 9 \times 10^{3} \times 2}{25}\)
\(= \dfrac{36}{25} \times 10^{3}\)
\(= 1.44 \times 10^{15}\) NC\(^{-1}\) along \(\overrightarrow{BP}\)
To calculate BP
\(\left|\overrightarrow{BP}\right| = (BA)\cos(45)^{\circ} = \dfrac{5}{\sqrt{2}}\)

subtopic: Electric Field and Lines of Force
stem: A simplified model of hydrogen atom consists of an electron revolving about a proton at a distance of \(5.3 \times 10^{-11}\)m. The charge on a proton is \(+1.6 \times 10^{-19}\) C. Calculate the intensity of the electric field due to proton at this distance.
solution:
\(E = \dfrac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_{o}r^{2}}\)
\(q = +1.6 \times 10^{-19}C\)
\(r = 5.3 \times 10^{-11}m\)
\(\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_{o}} = 9.0 \times 10^{9}Nm^{2}C^{-1}\)
\(E = \dfrac{1.6 \times 10^{-19}}{(5.3 \times 10^{-11})^{2}} \times 9.0 \times 10^{9} = 5.1 \times 10^{11}NC^{-1}\)
The force between electron and proton in hydrogen atom can be calculated by using the electric field. We have, \(E = \dfrac{F}{q}\ \therefore F = qE\)
F \(= -1.6 \times 10^{-19}\) C \(\times\) \(5.1 \times 10^{11}\) NC\(^{-1}\)
\(= -8.16 \times 10^{8}\) N.
This force is attractive.
Using the Coulomb's law,
\(F = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}}\dfrac{q_{1}q_{2}}{r^{2}}\)
\(= 9.0 \times 10^{9}Nm^{2}C^{-1} \times \dfrac{(-1.6 \times 10^{-19}C) \times (+1.6 \times 10^{-19}C)}{(5.3 \times 10^{-11}m)^{2}}\)
\(= -8.6 \times 10^{8}N\)
Knowing electric field at a point is useful to estimate the force experienced by a charge at that point.

stem: A charge of 5.0 C is kept at the centre of a sphere of radius 1 m. What is the flux passing through the sphere? How will this value change if the radius of the sphere is doubled?
solution:
Flux per unit area is given by Eq. 10.16.
According to Gauss law, the total flux through the sphere \(\Phi = \int \vec{E}.\vec{ds}\), where the integration is over the surface of the sphere. As the electric field is same all over the sphere i.e. \(|\vec{E}| =\) constant and the direction of \(\vec{E}\) as well as that of \(\vec{ds}\) is along the radius, we get
flux \(= \Phi = |E|4\pi R^{2}\)
\(E = \dfrac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}r^{2}} = 9 \times 10^{9} \times \dfrac{5.0\,\text{C}}{(1.0\,\text{m})^{2}}\)
\(E = 9 \times 10^{9} \times 5 = 4.5 \times 10^{10}\ \text{NC}^{-1}\)
\(\phi = \vec{E} \cdot \vec{S}\)
\(\therefore\) flux \(= 4.5 \times 10^{10} \times 4\pi(1)^{2}\)
\(= 5.65 \times 10^{11}\,\text{Vm}\)
Thus the total flux is independent of radius.
\(E \propto 1/r^{2}\), and area \(\propto r^{2}\). This can also be seen from Gauss' law, where the net flux crossing a closed surface is equal to \(q/\varepsilon_{0}\) where q is the net charge inside the closed surface. As the charge inside the sphere is unchanged, the flux passing through a sphere of any radius is the same. Thus, if the radius of the sphere is increased by a factor of 2, the net flux passing through its surface remains unchanged. As shown in Fig. 10.17, same number of lines of force cross both the surfaces. The total flux is independent of shape of the closed surface because Eq. 10.18 does not involve any radius.

stem: An electric dipole of length 2.0 cm is placed with its axis making an angle of \(30^{\circ}\) with a uniform electric field of \(10^{5}\) N/C. as shown in figure. If it experiences a torque of \(10\sqrt{3}\) Nm, calculate the magnitude of charge on the dipole.
solution:
Given
\(\tau = 10\sqrt{3}, Nm,\ E = 10^{5}N/C,\)
\(2l = 2.0 \times 10^{-2}m,\ \theta = 30^{0}\)
\(\tau = qE2l\sin\theta\)
\(10\sqrt{3}Nm = q10^{5}N/C\,2.0 \times 10^{-2}m\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\)
\(\therefore q = \dfrac{10\sqrt{3}}{10^{3}} = \sqrt{3} \times 10^{-2}C\)
\(= 1.73 \times 10^{-2}C\)
